d: Searchable glossary of academic terms and exam command words with definitions and examples.
Break something into parts and examine how those parts relate to each other.
Weigh strengths and limitations and reach a supported judgment.
Describe similarities and differences between two or more things.
Focus on the differences between two or more things.
Give reasons for how or why something happens.
Give an account of the main features of something.
Name or pick out something from information provided.
State the precise meaning of a term.
Consider several points of view or factors, with reasoning.
Support a decision or conclusion with reasons or evidence.
Explain the meaning or significance of information such as data, text or a graph.
Give the main points briefly.
Show how something works or is true, using evidence, examples or steps.
Work out a numerical answer, showing the steps.
Obtain a result or formula from earlier results through logical steps.
Sort items into groups according to shared features.
Judge the importance, quality or extent of something, weighing evidence.
Look closely at something and investigate its parts or details.
Give the main points or steps in brief.
Make a point clear by giving examples or a diagram.
Give a reasoned judgment of the strengths and weaknesses of something.
Show the difference between two or more things.
Draw a conclusion from evidence or reasoning rather than from a direct statement.
State what you expect to happen, based on knowledge or evidence.
Show with logical steps that a statement is true.
Give a brief, clear answer without explanation.
Put forward a possible idea or explanation, usually based on given information.
Establish an answer by calculation or from evidence.
Give an approximate value using reasonable assumptions.
Add detail, explanation or examples to a point.
A symbol, often a letter, representing a quantity that can change or is unknown.
A combination of numbers, variables and operations without an equals sign.
A statement that two expressions are equal.
A number that multiplies a variable.
A number or expression that divides another exactly.
A statement that compares two expressions using less than, greater than or similar signs.
A number that represents part of a whole, written as one number over another.
A comparison of two quantities showing how many times one contains the other.
A fraction expressed out of 100.
An equation that can be written as ax squared plus bx plus c equals 0, where a is not zero.
A solution of an equation, or a number that when multiplied by itself a given number of times gives a value.
The amount of surface a 2D shape covers.
The total distance around the outside of a 2D shape.
The amount of space inside a 3D object.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
An angle of exactly 90 degrees.
The sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when data is arranged in order.
The most frequent value in a data set.
The difference between the largest and smallest values.
A number from 0 to 1 that measures how likely an event is.
One possible result of a probability experiment.
A set of one or more outcomes in probability.
The process by which plants and some other organisms use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
The green pigment in plants that absorbs light for photosynthesis.
A simple sugar that cells use as a source of energy.
An organelle in plant and algal cells that contains chlorophyll and carries out photosynthesis.
The basic unit of structure and function in living organisms.
A structure inside a cell that has a specific function.
An organelle where aerobic respiration releases energy for the cell.
A push or pull on an object, measured in newtons.
The rate of change of velocity.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms.
The tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion.
Speed in a given direction.
The straight-line distance and direction from the start to the end point.
A representation of a chemical reaction using formulas.
A substance that is present at the start of a chemical reaction and is changed by it.
A substance formed in a chemical reaction.
A substance that produces hydrogen ions in water and has a pH below 7.
A substance that neutralises acids.
A scale, usually from 0 to 14, that measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
The reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water.
A testable explanation or prediction that evidence can support or contradict.
The variable you deliberately change in an experiment.
The variable you measure in an experiment.
A sentence that states the central, arguable claim of an essay.
A sentence that states the main idea of a paragraph.
A claim supported by reasons and evidence.
Facts, data, examples or sources used to support a claim.
Affect is usually a verb meaning to influence; effect is usually a noun meaning a result.
Their shows possession, there shows place or existence, and they're means they are.
Its shows possession; it's means it is or it has.
Then refers to time or sequence; than is used in comparisons.
Restate an idea from a source in your own words and sentence structure.
A reference in your text that shows where an idea, quotation or fact came from.
Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own.
The degree to which a source can be trusted.
A tendency to present or favour one point of view unfairly.
A figure of speech that describes one thing as if it were another, without like or as.
A figure of speech that compares two things using like or as.
A first-hand record created at the time of an event or by someone who experienced it.
A source created later that analyses or interprets primary sources.
The angle of a place north or south of the equator, in degrees.
The angle of a place east or west of the prime meridian, in degrees.
The line of latitude at 0 degrees that circles Earth midway between the poles.
A relationship where one event or factor brings about another.
A finite, ordered set of clear steps for solving a problem.
A structured way to describe an algorithm that looks like code but is not tied to any language.
A diagram that shows the steps of a process using shapes and arrows.
A named location in memory that stores a value which can change.
The kind of value a variable holds, such as integer, string or Boolean.
A sequence of characters, such as text.
A whole number, positive, negative or zero.
A data type with two possible values, true or false.
The repetition of a set of instructions.
The quantity of a good that buyers are willing and able to buy at each price.
The quantity of a good that sellers are willing and able to sell at each price.
The point where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
The condition that resources are limited while wants are unlimited.
The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
A situation where gaining more of one thing means having less of another.
A sustained rise in the general level of prices.
The price of borrowing money, or the return on saving it, expressed as a percentage.
A measure of the average change in prices of a basket of goods and services bought by households.
A relationship in which two variables tend to change together.
A third factor that influences both of the variables being studied and creates a misleading link.
An error in reasoning that weakens an argument.
